claims.claim: Oswald 'sent to the elders of the Scots, among whom himself and his followers, when in banishment, had received the sacrament of baptism, desiring they would send him a bishop'; 'sent him Bishop Aidan, a man of singular meekness, piety, and moderation'

'Scots' = Irish: Bede 'the Scots which dwelt in the South of Ireland' (GILES l.5757-5758); Huyshe's notes: 'the people of the Picts and that of the Scots of Britain [the Irish colonists in what is now Scotland]' and 'Thus Bede calls Aedan "King of the Scots," i.e. of the Irish who inhabit Britain'

'Bishop Aidan was himself a monk of the island called Hii, whose monastery was for a long time the chief of almost all those of the northern Scots'; III.5 'From the aforesaid island, and college of monks, was Aidan sent ... having received the dignity of a bishop at the time when Segenius, abbat and priest, presided over that monastery'
claims.witness: Bede, HE III.3, GILES l.5794-5797; III.5, l.5914-5918 (OCR '"P ROM the aforesaid island')

claims.claim: Came to the English in the 630s: derived from Bede's death year 651 (V.24 annals, GILES l.15317-15318) and his 'seventeenth year of his episcopacy' (III.17, l.6939) / 'Aidan was bishop seventeen years' (III.26, l.8240); the Bollandists: 'Ecclesia Lindisfarnensis a Rege Nordanhymbrorum S. Oswaldo fundata est anno DCXXXV, et S. Aidano Sedes Episcopalis ibidem erecta' The 630s rests on Bede's counts; the 635 is the Bollandists' year (Dominant Modern Reconstruction, the Bollandists).

Lindisfarne: 'the king appointed him his episcopal see in the isle of Lindisfarne ... Which place, as the tide flows and ebbs twice a day, is enclosed by the waves of the sea like an island; and again, twice in the day, when the shore is left dry, becomes contiguous to the land'

'when the bishop, who was not skilful in the English tongue, preached the gospel, it was most delightful to see the king himself interpreting the word of God to his commanders and ministers, for he had perfectly learned the language of the Scots during his long banishment'

Bede wrote c.731 from informants: 'This is for the present the state of all Britain; in the year since the coming of the English into Britain about 285, but in the 731st year of the incarnation of our Lord'; on Aidan: 'as near as I could be informed by those that knew him'. Some eighty years later is reckoned from 651 to 731.

'it was the highest commendation of his doctrine, with all men, that he taught no otherwise than he and his followers had lived'; 'He was wont to traverse both town and country on foot, never on horseback, unless compelled by some urgent necessity; and wherever in his way he saw any ... he invited them, if infidels, to embrace the mystery of the faith; or if they were believers, to strengthen them in the faith, and to stir them up by words and actions to alms and good works'

'whatsoever gifts of money he received from the rich, he either distributed them ... to the use of the poor, or bestowed them in ransoming such as had been wrongfully sold for slaves. Moreover, he afterwards made many of those he had ransomed his disciples, and after having taught and instructed them, advanced them to the order of priesthood'

'Eata was one of Aidan's twelve boys of the English nation, whom he received when first made bishop there, to be instructed in Christ'; 'This is the same Eata, who, not long after, was made bishop of the same church of Lindisfarne'; Eata 'abbat of the monastery of Melrose'. Bede gives the request to Oswy as what 'they say'.

Oswin's horse: 'He had given an extraordinarily fine horse to Bishop Aidan ... a poor man meeting him, and asking alms, he immediately dismounted, and ordered the horse, with all his royal furniture, to be given to the beggar'; king: 'Why would you, my lord bishop, give the poor man that royal horse ...?'; 'What is it you say, O king? Is that foal of a mare more dear to you than the Son of God?'; the king 'fell down at the bishop's feet, beseeching him to forgive him'; the bishop 'grew so melancholy as to shed tears. His priest then asking him, in the language of his country ... why he wept, "I know," said he, "that the king will not live long; for I never before saw so humble a king"'
claims.witness: Bede, HE III.14, GILES l.6761-6808 (OCR has a space before '?')

claims.claim: Oswin of Deira: 'Oswin, of the race of King Edwin ... who governed the province of the Deiri seven years'; killed by Oswy's command 'on the 20th of August'

Death: 'Not long after, the bishop's prediction was fulfilled by the king's death ... But Bishop Aidan himself was also taken out of this world, twelve days after the king he loved, on the 31st of August'; III.17 'He died in the seventeenth year of his episcopacy, the last day of the month of August'; annals: 'In the year 651, King Oswin was killed, and Bishop Aidan died'

Place of death: 'AIDAN was in the king's country-house, not far from the city of which we have spoken above, at the time when death separated him from his body, after he had been bishop sixteen years'; 'he gave up the ghost, leaning against a post that was on the outside to strengthen the wall'; 'His body was thence translated to the isle of Lindisfarne'. The city is the royal city 'which has its name from Bebba, formerly its queen' (III.16); L. Cecil Jane's note: '"The royal city" — Bamborough'
claims.witness: Bede, HE III.17, GILES l.6922-6942; III.16, l.6883-6885; Jane's note 149, l.15916 (prefatory note naming Jane as the Notes' author, l.15582-15586); OCR 'A IDAN', and Jane's note reads "' ' The royal city " — Bamborough."

claims.claim: Easter: 'he was wont to keep Easter Sunday according to the custom of his country ... from the fourteenth to the twentieth moon; the northern province of the Scots, and all the nation of the Picts, celebrating Easter then after that manner'; Bede: 'zealous in the cause of God, though not altogether according to knowledge'

Bede's side: 'in no way commending or approving what he imperfectly understood in relation to the observance of Easter; nay, very much detesting the same'; 'he always celebrated the same, not as some falsely imagine, on the fourteenth moon, like the Jews, whatsoever the day was, but on the Lord's day, from the fourteenth to the twentieth moon'

Bede followed the Roman Easter: III.3 the southern Irish 'by the admonition of the bishop of the Apostolic See, learned to observe Easter according to the canonical custom'; V.21 the English 'formed their religion after the example of the holy Roman Apostolic Church'

'This difference about the observance of Easter, whilst Aidan lived, was patiently tolerated by all men, as being sensible, that though he could not keep Easter contrary to the custom of those who had sent him, yet he industriously laboured to practise all works of faith, piety, and love ... and was held in veneration, not only by indifferent persons, but even by the bishops, Honorius of Canterbury, and Felix of the East Angles'

Charles Plummer: 'And yet we cannot help feeling that the question occupies a place in Bede's mind out of all proportion to its real importance. It is sad that he should think it necessary to pause in the middle of his beautiful sketch of the sweet and saintly character of Aidan to say that he "much detests" his mode of keeping Easter'

Anonymous Life of Cuthbert: 'in adolescentia sua ... cum aliis Pastoribus pecora domini sui pascebat ... vidit ... Angelos ascendentes et descendentes ... et inter manus eorum animam sanctam, quasi in globo igneo ad coelum efferri ... prophetans quoque eis animam esse sanctissimi Episcopi aut alterius magnae personae ... etenim post paucas dies, celeberrimum obitum sancti Episcopi nostri Aegdani, eadem hora noctis, qua ille viderat visionem, longe lateque nuntiatum esse audierunt'
claims.witness: 'Tertia Vita, Auctore monacho Lindisfarnensi coaevo', AASS-Mar3 l.38593-38596 (heading), l.38813-38832 (OCR 'ccelum', 'magnae perso- ns', 'celeherrimum', '4Egdani')

claims.claim: Bollandists date the anonymous Life: 'Videtur autem haec Vita conscripta, aut saltem absoluta, circa annum DCC'; its writer 'monachus Lindisfarnensis' (the Bollandists' own view: 'Videtur')

Bede's prose Life of Cuthbert: 'agnovitque mane facto Antistitem Lindisfarnensis Ecclesiae Aidanum, magnae utique virtutis virum, per id temporis, quo viderat, raptum de corpore, coelestia regna petiisse'

Bede's closing praise: 'his love of peace and charity; his continence and humility; his mind superior to anger and avarice ... his authority becoming a priest in reproving the haughty and powerful, and at the same time his tenderness in comforting the afflicted, and relieving or defending the poor'; 'These things I much love and admire in the aforesaid bishop; because I do not doubt that they were pleasing to God'
claims.witness: Bede, HE III.17, GILES l.6994-7011 (OCR 'dihgence' in the same list)

claims.claim: Traces: 'From that time many of the Scots came daily into Britain, and with great devotion preached the word to those provinces of the English, over which King Oswald reigned ... Churches were built in several places ... money and lands were given of the king's bounty to build monasteries ... for most of them that came to preach were monks' (OCR 'EngHsh')

'from ancient times, the bishop was wont to reside there with his clergy, and the abbat with his monks, who were likewise under the care of the bishop; because Aidan, who was the first bishop of the place, being himself a monk, brought monks thither, and settled the monastic institution there'
'many religious men and women, stirred up by his example, adopted the custom of fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays, till the ninth hour, throughout the year, except during the fifty days after Easter'

Chad: 'to travel about, not on horseback, but after the manner of the apostles, on foot, to preach the Gospel ... for he was one of the disciples of Aidan, and endeavoured to instruct his people, by the same actions and behaviour, according to his and his brother Cedd's example'

Hild (Hilda): 'Bishop Aidan being recalled home, he gave her the land of one family on the north side of the river Wear'; Heiu 'said to have been the first woman that in the province of the Northumbrians took upon her the habit and life of a nun, being consecrated by Bishop Aidan'; 'Bishop Aidan, and other religious men that knew her and loved her, frequently visited and diligently instructed her'. The Latin reads that Aidan called her home; Giles's English is ambiguous. Plummer's Latin: 'deinde ab Aidano episcopo patriam reuocata accepit locum unius familiae ad septentrionalem plagam Uiuri fluminis'.
claims.witness: Bede, HE IV.23, GILES l.10924-10946; PLUM l.24866-24868 (OCR 'Uiuri*'); OCR 'took, upon her'

claims.claim: Wonders: oil and storm, told 'by Cynemund, a most faithful priest of our church, who declared that it was related to him by Utta, the priest, on and by whom the same was wrought'; the fire at the royal city, 'related by many such as were likely to have knowledge thereof', with Aidan 'reported' to have said 'Behold, Lord, how great mischief Penda does!'; the post that 'could not be consumed by the fire' when the church burned, and again 'the second time'

Card otherNames: 'Aedan' (Plummer's Latin: 'accepit namque pontificem Aedanum', 'Monachus ipse episcopus Aedan', 'missus est Aedan'); 'Aidanus' (Bollandists, e.g. 'Colitur S. Aidanus primus illius Ecclesiae Episcopus 31 Augusti. Mortuus anno Christi 651'); 'Edanus' (Alcuin's poem, 'Praesulis Edani', and the note printed with the poem in Migne's volume 'Legendum Aidani, seu Edani (quo nomine vocatur carmine seq.)')

Alcuin's York poem retells the right-hand blessing: 'Tempore nam quodam praesul sanctissimus [Aedan] Cum rege et populo Paschalia festa peregit ... Vidit ut hoc praesul, dextram comprehendit, et infit: Incorrupta, precor, maneat manus ista per aevum'
claims.witness: ALC l.64991-64995 (title 'POEMA [DE] PONTIFICIBUS ET SANCTIS ECCLESIAE EBORACENSIS'), l.65627, 65646, 65656-65657 (OCR 'przsul', '[/Edan ]', 'Ineorrupta', '2»ivum')

claims.claim: Roman Breviary (Bute): calendar '31. Aidan, Bishop [of Lindisfarne,] Confessor. Double.'; martyrology: 'In England, [in the year 651,] holy Aidan, Bishop of Lindisfarne. Holy Cuthbert, who was then a shepherd lad, saw the soul of Aidan carried up into heaven, and he thereupon left his sheep and became a monk.'; Fourth Lesson 'From the Venerable Bede's History, iii. 3'
Bede's own source for Bede: born in the territory of Wearmouth and Jarrow; writing 'till the fifty-ninth year of my age'
Charles Plummer edited Bede's Historia in 1896: title page 'Venerabilis Baedae Historiam ecclesiasticam gentis Anglorum ... CAROLUS PLUMMER, A.M.', Oxford, Clarendon Press, MDCCCXCVI
claims.witness: PLUM l.60 (title page); file header l.1-4 gives the same

claims.claim: David of Menevia: Rees's note on Saint David, brought up at 'Hen Meneu, and in Latin Vetus Menevia', died 'in the Monastery he had founded in Menevia'; his disciple 'Maidoc, qui et Aidanus ab infantia' and 'his disciple Saint Aidan'
Aedan, king of the Scots in Britain: 'Hereupon, Aedan, king of the Scots that inhabit Britain'

contested_claims.claim: Whether Aidan's Easter reckoning deserved Bede's censure
sides: Bede: kept 'not altogether according to knowledge'; 'very much detesting the same', though always on the Lord's day (GILES l.5748, 6985-6988, 7026-7029)
Charles Plummer: the question 'occupies a place in Bede's mind out of all proportion to its real importance'; 'It is sad' that Bede pauses to say he detests it (PLUM l.2804-2809)

contested_claims.claim: When Cuthbert learned that the soul he saw was Aidan's
sides: Anonymous monk of Lindisfarne: 'post paucas dies' the news came (AASS-Mar3 l.38829-38832)
Bede's prose Life: 'mane facto', the next morning (AASS-Mar3 l.34343-34352)

absent_details.detail: Birth year, birthplace, age and family
absent_details.note: No held source gives them. Bede says only that he was sent from Iona by the Scots and kept 'the custom of his country'. Nothing written by Aidan himself is held or known from these sources.
Bede does not name him (GILES l.5967-5968).

No early Irish annals are held (the only Four Masters volume held covers 1172-1378). The Annales Cambriae name Aidan son of Gabran and a later Aidan son of Blegywryd, never Aidan of Lindisfarne (AC l.2572, 4241, 12204-12209).
Plummer's introduction mentions 'lives of SS. Aidan, Eata' in a Durham manuscript (PLUM l.9461); no such Life is held. The Acta Sanctorum volume for 31 August is not held.
Bede never gives the modern name; L. Cecil Jane's note gives 'Bamborough' for the royal city (GILES l.15916), and Plummer's index has '[Bebbanburg], Bamborough' (PLUM l.34868).

claims.claim: Caedmon, IV.24: 'There was in this abbess's monastery a certain brother'; at feasts 'when he saw the instrument come towards him, he rose up from table and returned home'; in sleep a person 'saluting him by his name, said, "Caedmon, sing some song to me." He answered, "I cannot sing"'; '"Sing the beginning of created beings," said the other. Hereupon he presently began to sing verses to the praise of God'; 'In the morning he came to the steward, his superior ... was conducted to the abbess, by whom he was ordered, in the presence of many learned men, to tell his dream, and repeat the verses'; 'the abbess ... instructed him to quit the secular habit, and take upon him the monastic life ... and ordered that he should be taught the whole series of sacred history'; 'Others after him attempted, in the English nation, to compose religious poems, but none could ever compare with him'. Latin 'In huius monasterio abbatissae fuit frater quidam' (PLUMMER l.25149, OCR 'monastcrio') ties him to Hild after IV.23. Giles OCR opens "'T^HERE was in this abbess's monastery".
claims.witness: GILES (bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt) l.11137-11218 (OCR 'C^dmon', 'In the English'; page break inside 'their [276] turns') [OCR forms: '^'Caedmon', 'T^HERE was in this abbess's monastery']

claims.claim: Whitby and its name: 'the monastery of Streaneshalch, which signifies the Bay of the Lighthouse, where the Abbess Hilda ... then presided'; Jane's note 'Streaneshalch = Whitby' (OCR "'WWithy"); Giles's bracket 'Streaneshalch [Whitby]'. Northumbria: she was 'the most religious servant of Christ' among 'the Northumbrians'; Paulinus 'the first bishop of the Northumbrians'
Bede is the main witness, writing in 731, fifty-one years after her death in 680 (computed from his last annal, 'In the year 731', l.15408, and l.10890-10896)

Birth and faith: 'she was nobly born, being the daughter of Hereric, nephew to King Edwin, with which king she also embraced the faith and mysteries of Christ, at the preaching of Paulinus'; Edwin baptized 'in the year of the incarnation of our Lord 627 ... at York, on the holy day of Easter, being the 12th of April'

Death and age: 'passed from thence ... on the 17th of November, at the age of sixty-six years; the first thirty-three of which she spent living most nobly in the secular habit'. Latin: 'die XV. Kalendarum Decembrium, cum esset annorum LXVI'. Birth about 614 is reckoned from these figures, not stated by Bede.

East Angles and Cale: 'she withdrew into the province of the East Angles, for she was allied to the king; being desirous to pass over from thence into France ... in the monastery of Cale ... because her sister Hercsuid ... at that time living in the same monastery, under regular discipline'; 'she continued a whole year in the aforesaid province, with the design of going abroad'. Latin: 'soror ipsius Heresuid ... annum totum in praefata prouincia retenta est; deinde ab Aidano episcopo patriam reuocata accepit locum unius familiae ad septentrionalem plagam Uiuri fluminis'. Giles's English 'Bishop Aidan being recalled home, he gave her the land of one family' misrenders the Latin.

Aidan of Lindisfarne: Oswald 'asking a bishop of the Scottish nation, had Aidan sent him, and granted him an episcopal see in the Isle of Lindisfarne'; 'Bishop Aidan was himself a monk of the island called Hii'

Heruteu: 'she was made abbess in the monastery called Heruteu, which monastery had been founded, not long before, by ... Heiu'; 'Bishop Aidan, and other religious men that knew her and loved her, frequently visited and diligently instructed her'; III.24 'Heruteu, or, "The island of the Hart,"' (Latin 'id est insula cerui', OCR 'corui'); Jane's note '192. Heruteu = Hartlepool' (OCR '7/ifrtt/(fw = Hartlepool'; p.192 is the III.24 page with Heruteu)
claims.witness: GILES (bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt) l.10931-10946, 7768-7770, 15949; PLUMMER (bede_opera-historica-v1-historia-abbatum-lat_plummer1896.txt) l.21153-21154 [OCR forms: 'id ost insula corui'; Jane note garbled '7/ifrtt/(fw = Hartlepool']

claims.claim: Whitby founded: IV.23 'she also undertook either to build or to arrange a monastery in the place called Streaneshalch'; III.24, after Oswy's victory [A.D. 655], his daughter Elfleda 'was put into the monastery, called Heruteu ... where, at that time, the Abbess Hilda presided, and, two years after, having acquired a possession of ten families, at the place called Streaneshalch, she built a monastery there'. Latin 'cui tunc Hild abbatissa praefuit. Quae post biennium ... ibi monasterium construxit' (OCR 'l)iennium', 'Ilild')

Men and women: Trumwine 'chose his own place of residence in the monastery, which we have so often mentioned, of men and women servants of God, at Streaneshalch'; IV.23 'the brothers came with news of her death'

Her rule: 'taught there the strict observance of justice, piety, chastity, and other virtues, and particularly of peace and charity; so that, after the example of the primitive church, no person was there rich, and none poor'; 'not only indifferent persons, but even kings and princes, as occasion offered, asked and received her advice'; reading of Scripture so that 'many might be there found fit for ecclesiastical duties, and to serve at the altar'

Five bishops: 'we afterwards saw five bishops taken out of that monastery ... Bosa, Hedda, Oftfor, John, and Wilfrid'; John 'bishop of Hagulstad', Wilfrid 'of the church of York'; Latin 'Bosa, Aetla, Oftfor, Iohannes, et Uilfrid'; Hagulstad = Hexham (Jane's note, OCR 'Hagul- j;aa'= Hexham'); Oftfor studied 'in both the monasteries of Hilda', went to Theodore and Rome, bishop in 'the province of the Wiccii'; Tatfrid 'from the same abbess's monastery' died before ordination; V.6 John 'ordained Wilfrid, his priest, bishop of the church of York'
claims.witness: GILES (bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt) l.10973-11013, 12539-12541, 15900-15902; PLUMMER (bede_opera-historica-v1-historia-abbatum-lat_plummer1896.txt) l.24946-24956 [OCR forms: 'Iohannes' as 'lohannes']

claims.claim: Mother: 'Abbess Hilda, whom all that knew her called Mother, for her singular piety and grace'; Latin 'quam omnes, qui nouerant, ob insigne pietatis et gratiae matrem uocare consuerant'; and she 'afforded occasion of amendment and salvation to many who lived at a distance, to whom the fame was brought of her industry and virtue'
claims.witness: GILES (bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt) l.11014-11020; PLUMMER (bede_opera-historica-v1-historia-abbatum-lat_plummer1896.txt) l.24994-24996 [OCR forms: 'ob msigne pietatis']

claims.claim: Synod of 664: 'it was agreed, that a synod should be held in the monastery of Streaneshalch ... The kings, both father and son, came thither'; 'controversy ... concerning Easter, or the tonsure'; 'the Abbess Hilda and her followers were for the Scots'; Latin 'Hild abbatissa cum suis in parte Scottorum' (Plummer margin 'a. 664'); Colman 'who was also sent out of Scotland'; Wilfrid's side with Agilbert, Agilbert asks that 'the priest Wilfrid, may speak in my stead'; Alfrid had given Wilfrid 'a monastery of forty families, at a place called Rhypum' (Jane: 'Rhypum ... = Ripon'); Oswy: 'he is the door-keeper, whom I will not contradict' and the company conforms; year: 'In the year 664 ... Colman returned to the Scots'
claims.witness: GILES (bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt) l.7955-7968, 7917, 7930-7941, 7996-7997, 8200-8218, 15326-15328, 15953; PLUMMER (bede_opera-historica-v1-historia-abbatum-lat_plummer1896.txt) l.21397-21413 [OCR forms: 'Hild abbatissa cum suis in paiie Scottorum']

claims.claim: The Scots as the people who sent Aidan: 'The same king Oswald, asking a bishop of the Scottish nation, had Aidan sent him'; Plummer, 'the Irish monks of Iona, by whom Northumbria was reconverted after the apostasy which followed the death of Edwin in 633' (card only)
claims.witness: GILES (bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt) l.5726-5728; PLUMMER (bede_opera-historica-v1-historia-abbatum-lat_plummer1896.txt) l.987-990 [OCR forms: 'asking- a bishop'; 'the Irish monks of lona']

claims.claim: Stephen's Life of Wilfrid, ch. 10: 'in coenobio quod Streuneshalgh dicitur, presente sanctimoniale matre piissima Hilde, presentibus quoque regibus, et duobus, Colmanno et Aegilberhto, episcopis, de Paschali ratione conquirebant' (OCR 'ganctimoniale', '/Egilberhto'; Raine margin '(Whitby)'). Raine calls him 'The first biographer of Wilfrid', who calls himself 'Stephanus presbyter'.
claims.witness: RAINE (byrhtferth_vita-s-oswaldi-in-historians-of-the-church-of-york-v1-lat_raine1879.txt) l.5067-5085, 1678-1697 [OCR forms: 'presente ... ganctimoniale matre piissima Hilde' with a margin note between]

claims.claim: Pope John's letter in Stephen, ch. 54, to 'Athelredo regi Merciorum, et Alfrido regi Derorum et Berniciorum': 'Dudum enim sub Apostolicae memoriae praedecessore nostro Agathone pontifice, dum Wilfrithus episcopus ad hanc sedem Apostolicam veniens appellasset; et praesentibus ejus contrariis, qui a Theodoro venerandae memoriae archiepiscopo sanctae Cantuariorum ecclesiae ... et Hylde religiosae memoriae abbatissae, ad eum accusandum huc prius advenerant' (OCR 'excellentissinis', 'hamo sedem', 'Hylde*'; apparatus 'Hylda] Hilde, A.'). Bede's History has no such account: every Hilda/Hild line in Giles (l.7769-7772, 7960-7967, 10888-11120, 11519, 15363) was read.

Illness and death: 'Falling into a fever ... afflicted with the same for six years continually; during all which time she never failed ... publicly and privately to instruct the flock'; 'having received the holy communion ... she admonished them to preserve evangelical peace among themselves, and with all others; and as she was making her speech, she joyfully saw death approaching'; V.24 'The same year also the Abbess Hilda died at Streaneshalch' (680)

Mother's dream: 'the dream which her mother, Bregusuit, had, during her infancy ... she found a most precious jewel under her garment, which ... cast such a light as spread itself throughout all Britain; which dream was brought to pass in her daughter that we speak of, whose life was a bright example, not only to herself, but to all who desired to live well' (Latin 'in infantia eius')

Visions at her death (card): Hackness 'which she had built that same year'; 'a certain nun called Begu'; 'she perceived that what she had seen was either in a dream or a vision'; 'It is also reported, that her death was, in a vision, made known the same night to one of the holy virgins ... in the same monastery'; Jane 'Hackness. Near Whitby'

Elfleda (card): Oswy 'gave his daughter Elfleda, who was scarce a year old'; 'the aforesaid king's daughter was first a learner, and afterwards a teacher of the monastic life'; 'she and her father, Oswy, her mother, Eanfleda, her mother's father, Edwin, and many other noble persons, are buried in the church of the holy Apostle Peter' (Giles 'being sixty years of age'; Latin 'undeLX', not used)
Caedmon's songs (card): 'By his verses the minds of many were often excited to despise the world, and to aspire to heaven'

Plummer: 'there are no scenes in the whole of Bede's histories over which he lingers so lovingly, as the holy deathbeds ... of Benedict Biscop, Sigfrid, Boisil, Chad, Hild and Caedmon' (OCR 'Csedmon'); 'the cowherd of St. Hilda's monastery'

Thomas of Ely, Life of Etheldreda I: 'Regina ... apud Gallias peregrina in monasterium Cale secessit ... Ad quam veniens et postea Hilda soror ipsius, relicta patria, ejus aemulata exemplum, in eodem monasterio peregrinam pro Domino vitam ducere volens; sed ab Aidano Episcopo post annum ad patriam revocata' (OCR 'Il.lda', 'ab d Aidano'); heading 'Auctore Thoma Monacho Elyensi'; Bollandists: 'cum ante finem seculi xii scripserit' (OCR 'scripse- rit')
York litany: '$ancta Hilda ora' (OCR '$' for S); Wordsworth: 'Cuthbert is addressed in the Sarum Prymer, but not Wilfrid, William, or Hilda, who appear in the York book'

claims.claim: Ceolfrid's letter: 'many of them have been holy and worthy of God. Of which number is Adamnan, the abbat and renowned priest of Columba, who, when sent ambassador by his nation to King Alfrid, came to see our monastery, and discovering wonderful wisdom, humility, and religion in his words and behaviour'; question: 'why do you, contrary to the habit of your faith, wear on your head a crown that is terminated, or bounded? And if you aim at the society of St. Peter, why do you imitate the tonsure of him whom St. Peter anathematised?'; answer: 'Be assured, my dear brother, that though I have Simon's tonsure, according to the custom of my country, yet I utterly detest and abhor the Simoniacal wickedness'
claims.witness: Ceolfrid, letter to King Naitan, in Bede HE V.21, GILES l.14879-14901 (OCR 're- nowned', 'Simoniacal' at l.14901)

claims.claim: Aldfrith of Northumbria: Huyshe's note, 'Aldfrid, Aldfrith, or Ealdfrith, the Northumbrian Prince, who succeeded his brother Ecgfrith as king in 685, was at the time of Adamnan's accession to the Abbacy of Iona, 679, a refugee in Ireland'; intro: 'When, eventually, Aldfrith came to the throne of Northumbria, Adamnan visited his court ... and presented to him his book De Locis Sanctis'

The letter's writer and abbey: 'Naitan, king of the Picts ... sent messengers to the venerable Ceolfrid, abbat of the monastery of the blessed apostles, Peter and Paul, which stands at the mouth of the river Wear, and near the river Tyne, at the place called Jarrow'; Bede gives the letter in full

Ceolfrid: 'This I then said to Adamnan, who indeed showed how much he had improved upon seeing the statutes of our churches, when, returning to Scotland, he afterwards by his preaching brought great numbers of that nation over to the catholic observance of the Paschal time; though he was not yet able to gain the consent of the monks that lived in the island of Hii, over whom he presided. He would also have been mindful to amend the tonsure, if his authority had extended so far.'

Huyshe: 'He was born in 624, twenty-seven years after the death of Columba, in south-western Donegal, descended from Sedna, an uncle of Columba, and was brought up in the monastic schools, and became a monk under his kinsman, Seghine, Abbot of Iona. In 679, in his fifty-fifth year, Adamnan succeeded to the chair of St. Columba, and to him there came as a refugee the English Prince Aldfrith, who was called the foster-son, or alumnus, of Adamnan.' No source is named in this passage.
claims.witness: Wentworth Huyshe, Introduction, HUY l.1979-1990 (line-break 'twenty- seven')

claims.claim: Huyshe: 'Adamnan was in Ireland in 692, and again in 697, on ecclesiastical and political business ... It is thought that he wrote the Life of St. Columba between the two visits. Adamnan seems to have remained in Ireland until 704, in which year he returned to his monastery in Iona, and there, soon after, he died.'

The Life's form: 'Adamnan's work is in three books ... The first book is upon the Saint's Prophetic Revelations, the Second upon his Miracles, the third, up to the twenty-third chapter, upon Angelic Visitations, and in the twenty-third chapter we have to the end one of the most exquisite pieces of pure biography'
Adomnán's preface: 'they should give credit to the facts therein recorded, and attend to the matter rather than to the words, which, as I think, seem uncultured and rude'
claims.witness: Adomnán, Life of Columba, first preface, HUY l.2082-2086

claims.claim: Failbe and Oswald: 'My predecessor, our Abbot Failbeus, related this narrative to me, Adamnan, nothing doubting, and he declared that he had heard it from the mouth of King Oswald himself as he related this same vision to Seghine, the Abbot'; Oswald 'sees St. Columba in a vision' the day before he fought Cation; Huyshe's notes: 'Oswald King of Northumbria, 635-642'; 'Our Abbot Failbeus Eighth Abbot of Iona, 669-679'
claims.witness: Life of Columba I.1, HUY l.2374-2424; notes l.2521-2537

claims.claim: Plague and Aldfrith: 'in Saxonia [England] also, on our visit to my friend, King Aldfrid, while the plague had not yet ceased and was devastating many villages up and down the country, the Lord, nevertheless, delivered us from danger ... so that not one of my own company died, nor was any one of them troubled by any disease'
claims.witness: Life of Columba II.46, HUY l.9120-9132 ('[England]' is Huyshe's gloss)

claims.claim: Cummene: 'Cuimine Ailbhe, surnamed also Fionn, or Albus, the Fair, seventh Abbot of Iona, 657-669. He wrote a book, "De virtutibus Sancti Columbae", which Adamnan has incorporated in this third book of his own work on the Saint.'

Bede: 'Adamnan, priest and abbat of the monks that were in the isle of Hii, was sent ambassador by his nation to Alfrid, king of the English, where he made some stay, observing the canonical rites of the church, and was earnestly admonished by many, who were more learned than himself, not to presume to live contrary to the universal custom of the Church, either in relation to the observance of Easter, or any other decrees ... in consequence of this he changed his mind'
claims.witness: Bede HE V.15, GILES l.13551-13562; Latin 'Siquidem Adamnan, presbyter et abbas monachorum, qui erant in insula Hii', PLUM l.27823-27824

claims.claim: 'For he was a good and wise man, and remarkably learned in Holy Scripture. Returning home, he endeavoured to bring his own people that were in the isle of Hii, or that were subject to that monastery, into the way of truth ... but in this he could not prevail. He then sailed over into Ireland ... he reduced many of them, and almost all that were not under the dominion of those of Hii, to the Catholic unity'

'Returning to his island, after having celebrated the canonical Easter in Ireland ... it so happened that he departed this life before the next year came round, the Divine goodness so ordaining it, that as he was a great lover of peace and unity, he should be taken away to everlasting life before he should be obliged, on the return of the time of Easter, to quarrel still more seriously with those that would not follow him in the truth'

Holy Places: 'This same person wrote a book about the holy places, most useful to many readers; his authority ... was Arculf, a French bishop, who had gone to Jerusalem ... travelled to Damascus, Constantinople, Alexandria, and many islands, and returning home by sea, was by a violent storm forced upon the western coast of Britain ... he presently committed to writing all that Arculf said ... Adamnan presented this book to King Alfrid ... The writer thereof was also well rewarded by him'; 'I believe it will be acceptable to our readers if we collect some particulars from the same, and insert them in our History'

De Locis Sanctis preface: 'In nomine Patris ... texere librum de locis incipio sanctis. Arculfus sanctus episcopus, gente Gallus ... in Hierosolymitana civitate per menses novem hospitatus ... mihi Adamnano haec universa quae infra exaranda sunt experimenta diligentius perscrutanti, et primo in tabulas describenti, fideli et indubitabili narratione dictavit'

contested_claims.claim: Who wrote the Historia Brittonum: Nennius, disciple of Elbotus, or another compiler
sides: For Nennius: the work's own prologue and apology in J. A. Giles's text (NEN l.42-43, 107-110); Hugh Williams writes of 'the Historia Britonum of Nennius' (GILDAS l.966-967); W. H. Stevenson calls Nennius 'the only other Welsh writer of this century known to us' (ASSER l.4290-4291)

Against or doubting: the heading 'edited by Mark the anchorite' (NEN l.170); Louis Duchesne, a Vatican copy under Mark the anchorite's name, and 'pseudo-Nennius' (LP1 l.52070-52071, 27343-27344); James Raine, 'the pseudo-Nennius' (RAINE l.1216); copies that give the book to Gildas, and Geoffrey of Monmouth quoting it as Gildas's, as Hugh Williams reports (GILDAS l.966-968)
